title: The road to monster fighting and upgrade in React life cycle
summary: The evolution of react life cycle
markdown:
>Excuse me! Don’t miss it if you pass by!
So far, React has released the v16.12.0 version. The React life cycle is also a daily development process. You can see the dog when you lower your head and see it when you look up. Unfortunately, the dog has changed.
## Reason for change
Prior to v16.3, update operations in React were synchronous, which could cause performance issues.
For example, if there is a huge module with many components nested in it, once the top render method is executed, the render methods of the components will be executed in sequence until the bottom component. This process will cause the main thread to get stuck.
In order to solve this problem, the official introduced React Fiber. The solution is sharded execution. An update process is divided into two phases: the first phase, Reconciliation Phase, and the second phase, Commit Phase.
In the first phase, Reconciliation Phase, React Fiber will find out which DOM needs to be updated. This phase can be interrupted; but in the second phase, Commit Phase, it will update the DOM in one go and will never be interrupted.
These two stages also correspond to different life cycles:
first stage
-componentWillMount
- componentWillReceiveProps
- shouldComponentUpdate
- componentWillUpdate
second stage
- componentDidMount
- componentDidUpdate
-componentWillUnmount
Take a look at this example: Fiber vs Stack Demo
## Change comparison
Previously:
![image]()
Now (v16.3):
![image]()
Comparing the upper and lower pictures, we find that React has abandoned the following methods:
-componentWillMount
- componentWillReceiveProps
- componentWillUpdate
It needs to be explained here: In order to achieve version compatibility, the UNSAFE_componentWillMount, UNSAFE_componentWillReceiveProps and UNSAFE_componentWillUpdate methods are added. Both the old and new methods can be used, but when using the old method, there will be a red warning in development mode, and it will be completely abandoned when React v17 is updated.
The following new methods have been added:
- getDerivedStateFromProps
- getSnapshotBeforeUpdate
## Stage sorting
The following is a summary of the life cycle methods from the three stages (mount, update, and uninstall).
![image]()
### constructor constructor
If you need to perform some initialization operations, such as initializing the state, otherwise there is no need to implement a constructor for the React component.
### getDerivedStateFromProps
This method replaces componentWillMount() when the component is instantiated, and componentWillReceiveProps() and componentWillUpdate() when new props are received.
```javascript
static getDerivedStateFromProps(nextProps, prevState)
```
In the v16.3 version, this method will not be called after re-rendering, but in the v16.4 version, this method will be called after re-rendering. This means that even if the props have not changed, once the parent component is re-rendered, the method of the child component will still be called.
### componentWillMount/UNSAVE_componentWillMount (soon to be deprecated)
Some students usually put data requests in this method to quickly obtain and display the data. However, in fact, no matter how fast the request is, it cannot be faster than the first render. Moreover, due to the execution mechanism of React Fiber, this method will be executed multiple times, which also means that the interface is requested multiple times. Therefore, this method will be completely abandoned after version v17.
### componentDidMount
Called after the component is mounted, and only called once globally. You can use refs here to get the real dom elements. Asynchronous requests can also be initiated within this hook, and setState can be performed during asynchronous requests.
### componentWillReceiveProps/UNSAFE_componentWillReceiveProps (soon to be deprecated)
Replaced by getDerivedStateFromProps method.
### shouldComponentUpdate
After each call to setState, shouldComponentUpdate will be called to determine whether the component needs to be re-rendered. Returns true by default and needs to be re-rendered. Return false to not trigger rendering. In more complex applications, some data changes do not affect the interface display. You can make judgments here to optimize rendering efficiency.
### componentWillUpdate
It is still due to the React Fiber execution mechanism. Recording DOM status in this method is no longer accurate.
### getSnapshotBeforeUpdate
The time when this method is triggered is the moment before the DOM is updated, which is more precise than the DOM state recorded by componentWillUpdate.
### componentDidUpdate
Except componentDidMount is called after the first render, componentDidUpdate is called after all other renders.
### componentWillUnmount
Called when the component is uninstalled. Generally, events registered in componentDidMount need to be deleted here.
## Summary
Because React updates components synchronously, it can cause performance problems and cause the main thread to get stuck. Therefore, React Fiber is introduced to reimplement the core algorithm. Then I discovered that React Fiber would cause some life cycle methods to be executed multiple times, so these methods were abolished and new methods were introduced.
